name: Tezcatlipoca
role: Smoking Mirror, god of night, fate and royal power
fun_fact: His name means Smoking Mirror, and his obsidian mirror was thought to show hidden thoughts and futures.

name: Quetzalcoatl
role: Feathered Serpent, god of wind, learning and creation
fun_fact: He is one of the few Mesoamerican gods also remembered as a legendary priest-king of Tollan.

name: Coatlicue
role: Serpent Skirt, earth mother of the gods
fun_fact: Her name means Serpent Skirt, and her colossal statue in Mexico City's National Museum of Anthropology is one of the most famous works of Aztec sculpture.

name: Huitzilopochtli
role: Hummingbird of the Left, patron god of the Mexica, war and the sun
fun_fact: He was born fully armed, according to the Florentine Codex, and his shrine stood at the top of the Templo Mayor beside Tlaloc's.

name: Coyolxauhqui
role: Moon goddess and leader of the four hundred stars
fun_fact: Her name is often translated as She of the Golden Bells, and the great stone showing her dismembered body was found in Mexico City in 1978.

name: Tlaloc
role: God of rain, thunder and the waters that feed the earth
fun_fact: His helpers, the tlaloque, were thought to pour rain from jars kept in the mountains, and thunder was the sound of those jars breaking.

name: Mictlantecuhtli
role: Lord of Mictlan, the land of the dead
fun_fact: He tried to keep Quetzalcoatl from taking the bones of the old people, and the story makes death the boundary that no one escapes.

name: Tonatiuh
role: The sun god, especially the sun of the fifth age
fun_fact: His face is at the center of the Aztec sun stone, surrounded by the signs of the earlier ages and the date Four Movement.

name: Xolotl
role: Quetzalcoatl's twin, guide of the dead and god of the evening star
fun_fact: His name is linked to the axolotl, the salamander that stays in the water, and dogs were buried with the dead to guide them.

name: Chicomecoatl
role: Seven Serpent, goddess of maize and the harvest
fun_fact: Her name means Seven Serpent, and she was honored in festivals that followed the planting and harvesting of maize.
